source.title: Recursive Inference Scaling: A Winning Path to Scalable Inference in Language and Multimodal Systems

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some figures and tables are flattened; numerical curve values are not recoverable from the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study fits held-out language-model loss against training compute, a different experimental setup from the original scaling-law studies: it holds model size fixed and varies recursive architecture and compute.
record.gate_note: The paper tests power-law scaling of log-perplexity with training FLOPs for 600M-parameter models, and compares architectures at matched compute. Downstream-task and multimodal results are reported, but they do not test whether scaling laws predict downstream performance or whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities. The vision experiment concerns supervised image classification, not held-out language-model loss. Curve values are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The scaling-law fits are a tool for comparing recursive architectures. One result bears on a version: the fitted exponent c and asymptote ε∞ of a loss-vs-compute power law shift with recursion depth r in 600M language models (Fig. 5a). That fits V7 (exponents depend on setup). No goodness-of-fit is reported for V1, and the architecture comparisons concern parameter sharing at matched compute, not depth/width shape (V4).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that, at matched model size and training compute, RINS beats 55+ parameter-sharing variants in language modelling. They also find that it improves both the scaling exponent and the asymptotic log-perplexity, that the optimal r grows with compute, and that it gives multimodal gains but no gain in supervised vision. With linear adapters, stochastic RINS is a no-regret pretraining choice.
record.recipe_differences: Uses power-law fits of held-out log-perplexity versus training FLOPs, but fixes parameter count and studies recursion architectures rather than separately varying parameters, tokens, and compute as in the original scaling-law work.
record.method_sensitivity: Fitted scaling exponent and asymptotic loss change with recursion count; the paper also reports that the optimal recursion count increases with training compute.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched parameter count and training FLOPs, RINS recursion (A^rB) lowers held-out log-perplexity vs the baseline and RAO. The gap widens with compute, though the baseline is better at low compute.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-matched recursive parameter sharing changes the loss-vs-compute curve of fixed-size LMs.

fits_no_version.finding: The loss-minimising recursion count r rises monotonically with training compute; smaller models benefit more (Fig. 5b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute-optimal recursion depth grows with compute budget.

record.problems: The relevant power-law curve values and fitted parameters are shown only in plots, without stated numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The scaling-law fit is reported for 600M-parameter models and training FLOPs, so it does not establish scaling across parameter and token counts.

untested.parts: Whether loss follows a power law: no fit quality is reported, model size is fixed, and the compute range is about one order of magnitude.
Parameter/token split. Only the optimal recursion count vs compute is studied.
No power-law fits for SigLIP or ViT.
Downstream scores are reported but not modelled against scale or loss.
Fitting method, parameter counting, schedule, and disagreement between published laws.

missing.what: The fitted coefficient β_r increases with r, alongside c_r rising and ε_r falling.
missing.locator: Section 6, Optimal Number of Recursion Rounds

missing.what: Optimal r vs training compute for 300M, 600M and 1B models.
Asymptotic (infinite-compute) loss of 1B stochastic-RINS models; this assumes a power law rather than testing it.

record.verdict_notes: The power-law fits are a tool here. The paper even states a power law is assumed for the asymptotic analysis. All curve values are figure only. The V7 support is weak: the setup dependence shown is architectural, not a fitting choice.

versions.untested_parts: Tests scaling against training FLOPs for fixed-size language models; does not independently test scaling against parameter count or token count.
Does not report fitting on small runs and predicting the losses of runs orders of magnitude larger.
Studies an optimal recursion count as compute changes, not the loss-minimising parameter-count/token-count split.
Tests parameter-sharing and recursion architectures at matched size and compute; does not systematically isolate depth, width, or other architecture details across a wide range.
Reports multimodal and vision performance comparisons, but does not fit or test power-law loss scaling in those regimes.
Evaluates downstream tasks, but does not test whether their performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
Shows that fitted scaling parameters vary with recursion depth; does not test other fitting choices, disagreement between published laws, or departures from a single power law.

relationships.condition: 600M decoder LMs, signature A^rB, r=2–4 vs r=1, C4 and SlimPajama, compute-matched
relationships.reason: The fitted exponent c rises and ε∞ falls with r, so the fitted law depends on architecture setup (EXP-*-r2..r4, ASY-*-r2..r4). Values are figure only.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing recursive depth from r=1 to r=2–4 raised the fitted exponent c and lowered ε∞ in compute-matched 600M models on C4 and SlimPajama.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: 600M-parameter language models; fixed model size; training-FLOPs sweeps on C4 and SlimPajama; recursion counts r=1,2,3,4
reader_labels.reason: The authors fit log-perplexity to the stated power-law form as a function of training FLOPs for these settings (PL-C4-r1–PL-C4-r4; PL-SP-r1–PL-SP-r4). This supports the compute-axis part tested, not parameter- or token-axis scaling.

reader_labels.reason: The text reports RINS outperforming the other architectures in the tested comparisons, rather than architecture changes having only slight effects (ARCH-300-C4, ARCH-300-SP, ARCH-600-C4, ARCH-600-SP).

reader_labels.label: supports
